opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Long-horizon stability is really the crux of it. When you build a data-driven model for weather, you're often judged on a few days or a couple of weeks of forecast skill. Climate is a different regime. You're rolling the model out autoregressively for years, even decades, and any small bias or instability compounds. You can get blow-ups, where the energy in the system grows without bound. You can also get the opposite, where everything smooths out and you lose the extremes and variability that matter most for climate.

So the first thing I think about is the architecture itself. That's a big part of why we've worked on neural operators. Instead of learning a mapping on a fixed grid, you learn an operator between function spaces. That gives you resolution invariance and a better inductive bias for the underlying continuous physics. On the sphere in particular, using spherical harmonics, as with the spherical Fourier neural operator, respects the geometry of the planet. You avoid artifacts at the poles and get much more stable rollouts than with naive approaches that treat the globe as a flat image.

The second piece is bringing physics into training and evaluation, not just data. Data alone is never enough, especially when you're extrapolating to future climate states you haven't observed. You want the model to respect conservation laws like mass and energy, and you want it to get the spectra right across scales. One approach is physics-informed losses, where you penalize violations of the governing PDEs. Another is to combine coarse-resolution data with the equations themselves, so the model is constrained even where data is sparse.

Third, you have to evaluate the right things. Pointwise error over a short window isn't the right metric for climate. You care about the statistics: the climatology, the variability, the tails, things like extreme events, and whether the model reproduces known phenomena and teleconnections over long runs. A model can look great on RMSE and still drift badly over a hundred-year simulation.

Finally, there's uncertainty. Climate is inherently about distributions, so generative and probabilistic approaches, plus large ensembles, are essential. One of the exciting things about these AI models is that they're orders of magnitude faster than traditional numerical solvers. That means you can actually run the huge ensembles you need to characterize risk, which was prohibitively expensive before.

So I see it as a combination of the right inductive biases, physical constraints, the right evaluation metrics, and honest uncertainty quantification. The goal isn't to replace physics. It's to build AI that's grounded in physics, so we can trust it when we push it into regimes that matter for policy and adaptation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So this is really the central problem, and I think it's underappreciated by people coming at it purely from the machine learning side. Weather forecasting and climate simulation look similar on the surface, but they're fundamentally different problems in terms of what reliability means.

For weather, you're rolling out maybe ten days. You can train on reanalysis data, compare against ground truth, and if your model like FourCastNet has small errors that accumulate, it doesn't matter much because you reinitialize from new observations anyway. For climate, you want to run decades or centuries into the future, and there is no ground truth to correct you. So any small bias in the model, any slight violation of conservation of mass or energy, compounds step after step. You can end up with a simulation that drifts, blows up, or worse, stays plausible-looking while being quantitatively wrong. That last failure mode is the dangerous one.

So the way I think about it is in a few layers. The first is architectural. Neural operators, which we developed to learn mappings between function spaces rather than between fixed grids, give you resolution invariance and a much better inductive bias for PDEs than a generic vision transformer. The Fourier neural operator captures the global, multi-scale structure of these dynamics in a way that's very natural for fluids on a sphere. That alone reduces the spurious high-frequency artifacts that tend to seed instability in long rollouts.

The second layer is physics constraints. You don't want to rely on the network accidentally learning conservation laws from data. You want to bake them in, either as hard constraints in the architecture, or as soft penalties in the loss, or through hybrid approaches where the learned component only handles the parts of the system we can't resolve, like clouds and convection, while the resolved dynamics still come from a physics core. Hybrid models are, I think, where a lot of the near-term value is for climate, because they inherit stability guarantees from the numerical solver while getting speed and fidelity gains from learning.

The third layer is training methodology. If you only train on one-step prediction, the model never sees its own errors, and then at inference time it's operating out of distribution within a few hundred steps. So we do multi-step autoregressive fine-tuning, we inject noise, we think about spectral properties of the predictions and make sure the energy spectrum isn't collapsing or blowing up at small scales. There's a lot of practical engineering here that matters as much as the architecture.

And then the fourth, which people often skip, is evaluation. You can't just report RMSE at a few lead times. You need to run thousands of years of simulation and check the climatology, the variability, the extremes, the response to forcing. Does the model reproduce El Niño statistics? Does it respond correctly if you double CO2? Those are the tests that tell you whether it's a climate model or just a very good interpolator.

Ultimately I think the goal is not to replace physics with a black box. It's to use learning where physics is incomplete or too expensive, and keep physics where it gives us guarantees. That combination is what will make these models trustworthy enough for people to actually make decisions based on them.

r001.rationale: It proposes baking conservation laws into the architecture, adding loss penalties, or using hybrid models to improve reliability in long simulations.

r002.rationale: It discusses high-frequency artifacts and monitoring small-scale energy spectra, but does not explain that preserving fine-scale detail can conflict with physical validity.

astra-6.text:
The challenge is that a model can look very accurate over a short forecast and still drift into an unphysical state when you run it for years. Small errors feed back into the simulation. So getting the next step right is necessary, but it’s not sufficient.

We need to bring physics into how we build and train these models—constraints like conservation of mass and energy—and then evaluate what happens over long rollouts. Does the model reproduce the right climate statistics? Does it capture extremes and the interactions between processes operating at different scales? A stable simulation alone doesn’t guarantee a physically correct one.

And for climate, we also have to ask whether the model responds correctly as the forcing changes. Reproducing the historical climate is only part of the problem. My view is that AI and numerical simulation should work together, combining what we know about the governing physics with what we can learn from data, and being explicit about the uncertainty.

r001.rationale: It proposes incorporating physical constraints such as mass and energy conservation into model building and training, then evaluating long rollouts for physical reliability.

r002.rationale: It mentions interactions across scales, but does not say that preserving fine-scale detail can conflict with physical validity.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge is that a model can make a very accurate short-term prediction and still drift into an unphysical state when you run it for decades. Small errors accumulate, and the model’s own predictions become its next inputs. So short-term accuracy alone doesn’t establish that you have a reliable climate simulator.

You want to build physical structure into the model—things like conservation of mass and energy—and then test whether those properties hold over long rollouts. You also need to ask whether it reproduces the right statistics: seasonal cycles, variability, extremes, and the interactions between different scales. Matching an average temperature is not enough.

And there’s a distinction between remaining stable and responding correctly to a changing climate. A model could be stable simply because it keeps returning to familiar conditions. We need to evaluate whether it responds appropriately when the forcing changes, and understand where its uncertainty grows. I see this as combining the strengths of physics-based simulation and machine learning, with careful validation over the timescales we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response proposes building physical structure into the model, including mass and energy conservation, and checking those properties over long rollouts.
